drills.title: vs Arundhamizh-vel (800) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's pieces on c3 and d3 were both already trained on e4, so any piece that jumps there needs at least two defenders, and your knight only had the d5 pawn covering it. Ne4 walked straight into that: Nxe4 grabbed the piece, and after ...Qd8 White simply tucked the knight to safety with N4g3, leaving you down a full piece from a comfortable +1.1. Nbd7 was the calm answer — finish developing first, and only jump into e4 once it's properly supported, as in Nbd7 Rd1 Re8 Ne4!, where a later grab is met by ...Qxd2 and the position stays balanced. Principle: before hopping into an outpost, count the attackers and defenders on that square first.

drills.coachNote: Black's plan was to lure your king forward so the rook on f2 could swing to d2 — with your own pawns on c3 and e3, plus Black's pawn on d5, boxing you in, there'd be no flight square at all. Principle: before advancing an exposed king, always scan for the opponent's rook checks first.

Bxc6 straight away was cleaner: after Bxc6, Qxc6 you're simply up a piece, and lines like Qf5, dxe5, Bxe5 show you keeping full control. When you're up this much, shut down the opponent's last active piece before you do anything else.

drills.coachNote: This position was never about material — Black's king is stuck out in the open on f6 with nothing around it, and the real prize is getting your pieces there faster than he can find cover, using something like the knight on c4 to jump into e5 or d7. Qxb7 grabbed the bishop, which felt free, but it cost you the one thing you couldn't spare: a tempo. Black used it to play Qd5, then Qc7 and Qd8, tucking the queen back and giving the king some breathing room, and your crushing +10.3 shrank by almost four pawns. Ne5 was the move that kept the pressure on — it threatens Nd7+ forking king and queen, and after Qe8 Rc7 Nd7+ Kg5 you're dragging Black's king into the open for a real mating attack. When the enemy king is this exposed, count attackers, not pawns.

drills.coachNote: Black's queen on d5 is doing quiet work here — it sits on the d5-e4-f3 diagonal, so it can meet any check on f3 by simply capturing. Qf3+ walked right into that: Qxf3 gxf3 traded queens off, and while you're still doing fine, Black got to activate with Rh8 down the h-file, costing you a big slice of your advantage (from a crushing +8.5 down almost three pawns). Clear away the defender before you deliver the check — don't hand your opponent the trade that bails him out.
